title: IELTS Academic Reading Practice Test 7
instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on each passage. Answer all 40 questions.

passages.title: The Urban Heat Island
passages.text:
A. Anyone who has walked from a shaded park into the centre of a large city on a summer evening has felt the phenomenon that meteorologists call the urban heat island. Built-up areas are consistently warmer than the countryside surrounding them — typically by one to three degrees Celsius during the day, and by as much as twelve degrees on a still, cloudless night. The effect was first described in 1818 by Luke Howard, an amateur meteorologist who compared temperature readings taken in London with those from the fields beyond it. Howard noticed something that continues to define the field: the difference between city and country was far greater after sunset than at midday.

B. The primary cause lies in the materials from which cities are made. Asphalt, brick and concrete have a low albedo, meaning they reflect only a small fraction of the sunlight falling on them and absorb the rest as heat. They also possess considerable thermal mass, storing that heat through the afternoon and releasing it slowly overnight. Rural land behaves quite differently. Vegetation and moist soil lose much of their absorbed energy through evapotranspiration — the combined evaporation of water from the ground and its release from the leaves of plants — which converts solar energy into water vapour instead of heat. Every hectare of ground sealed beneath a car park removes that cooling mechanism entirely.

C. A second contributor is the shape of the city itself. Tall buildings lining a narrow street form what climatologists term a street canyon. Sunlight entering such a canyon is reflected repeatedly between the facing walls, and each reflection transfers a little more energy into the fabric of the buildings. At night the same geometry works against cooling: a surface can only radiate heat to the portion of sky it can actually see, and in a deep canyon that portion is small. To this must be added the waste heat generated by the city's own activity — engines, industrial processes and, in a particular irony, the air conditioners installed to make overheated buildings habitable.

D. The consequences are not merely a matter of comfort. During the European heatwave of August 2003, mortality rose sharply in urban centres while nearby rural districts were far less affected. Heat stress is most dangerous when night-time temperatures fail to drop, denying the body the chance to recover, and it is precisely night-time cooling that the heat island suppresses. Nor is the burden shared evenly within a city. Studies in several countries have found that wealthier districts tend to have significantly more tree cover than poorer ones, so the residents least able to afford air conditioning are often those living in the hottest streets.

E. Measuring the effect is less straightforward than it appears. Fixed weather stations are reliable but sparse, and a single instrument in a park may not represent the neighbourhood around it. Researchers therefore supplement them with mobile transects, driving instrumented vehicles along a fixed route at the same hour on successive nights. Satellites offer a third approach, but a crucial caveat applies: thermal sensors in orbit record the temperature of surfaces — rooftops, roads, tree canopies — rather than the temperature of the air that people actually breathe. The two are correlated but not interchangeable, and conflating them has produced some overstated claims.

F. Mitigation is possible and, in places, already underway. Coating roofs in reflective paint raises their albedo and can lower indoor temperatures noticeably in the storeys immediately below. Planting street trees addresses the problem more directly still, restoring both shade and evapotranspiration; the network of green corridors created in Medellín, Colombia, has been credited with reducing local temperatures by around two degrees. Neither remedy is free of complications. Trees require water, which may be scarce in exactly the climates where cooling matters most, and highly reflective roofs that are welcome in July will increase heating demand in January. The most effective schemes tend to be those designed for a particular city rather than imported wholesale from another.

passages.title: The Mapmaker's Craft
passages.text:
A. A map is never simply a picture of the world. It is an argument about what matters in that world — a selection, made by someone, of the handful of features worth recording out of the countless features that exist. The oldest surviving artefact generally accepted as a map of the wider world is a Babylonian clay tablet of around the sixth century BCE, which places the city of Babylon at the centre of a circular landmass ringed by water. Its geography is poor by any modern standard. Its purpose, however, was never to guide a traveller, and judged as a statement about where the centre of things lay it is perfectly accurate.

B. The decisive intellectual step was taken in Alexandria in the second century CE, when Claudius Ptolemy compiled his Geographia. Ptolemy proposed that every place could be fixed by a pair of numbers — latitude and longitude — and he supplied coordinates for some eight thousand locations. Many were badly wrong, since he depended on travellers' estimates of distance, and he adopted an under-estimate of the Earth's circumference that would still be misleading sailors more than a millennium later. But the principle was sound and it proved durable. The Geographia was effectively lost to western Europe for centuries and survived through copies preserved and studied by Arabic scholars, returning to European hands only in the fifteenth century.

C. Running alongside this scholarly tradition was a wholly practical one. From the thirteenth century, Mediterranean sailors used portolan charts: coastal outlines of remarkable accuracy, criss-crossed by lines radiating from compass roses. These rhumb lines allowed a navigator holding a steady compass bearing to lay a course directly between two ports. What is striking about the portolans is that they owe almost nothing to theory. Nobody calculated them. They accumulated slowly from the recorded experience of people who had actually sailed the coasts they depict, and their inland detail is correspondingly vague.

D. In 1569 Gerardus Mercator published the projection that still bears his name, and in doing so accepted a bargain that cartographers have debated ever since. No flat sheet can represent a sphere without distorting something. Mercator chose to preserve angles, so that a straight line drawn on his chart corresponds to a constant compass bearing — an enormous practical gain for navigation. The price is area: landmasses far from the equator are inflated, which is why Greenland can appear comparable in size to Africa when it is in fact around fourteen times smaller. The projection was designed for sailors and remains excellent for them; the objection is to its use as a general picture of the world.

E. By the eighteenth century, mapping had become an instrument of the state. The Cassini family spent four generations surveying France by triangulation, a method that fixes positions by measuring the angles of a chain of triangles anchored to a single carefully measured baseline. Britain's Ordnance Survey was established in a similar spirit, its very name recording a military origin. Such surveys were expensive, slow and strategically valuable, and they made the map an assertion of authority as much as a description of terrain: to survey a territory precisely was, in part, to claim the right to administer it.

F. The digital era has changed who draws maps rather than abolishing the older questions. Satellite positioning has made accurate location almost free, and projects such as OpenStreetMap are compiled by volunteers rather than by state agencies. Yet the fundamental act remains one of selection. A routing application that omits a footpath has, for its users, effectively removed that footpath from the world. The technology is new; the question of who decides what appears on the map is as old as the Babylonian tablet.

passages.title: How Birds Learn to Sing
passages.text:
A. Biologists distinguish between a bird's calls and its song. Calls are typically brief, produced by both sexes and used for immediate purposes — warning of a predator, keeping a flock together. Song is longer, more elaborate and usually associated with defending a territory or attracting a mate. The distinction matters because the two are acquired in quite different ways. Calls are largely innate, appearing in more or less their adult form without any need for a model. Song, in the group of birds known as oscine songbirds — roughly half of all bird species — must be learned from other individuals, and a bird prevented from hearing one will never sing normally.

B. That learning follows a sequence with a striking resemblance to the acquisition of human speech. A young songbird first produces subsong: rambling, quiet and highly variable, with little recognisable structure. This gives way to plastic song, in which fragments of the adult pattern begin to appear but remain unstable and are rehearsed in many versions. Finally the song crystallises, becoming fixed and repeatable, and in many species it will scarcely change thereafter. The parallel with a human infant's babbling, gradually converging on the sounds of a particular language, has been drawn so often that the two fields now borrow terminology from one another.

C. The experimental foundation of this account was laid by W. H. Thorpe, who in the 1950s raised chaffinches in acoustic isolation. Birds deprived of an adult model produced song that was recognisably chaffinch-like in its broad outline but abnormally simple, lacking the fine structure of the wild form. Later work established that learning is confined to a sensitive period early in life, that a bird will preferentially copy the song of its own species when offered a choice, and that hearing itself is essential: a young bird deafened before crystallisation cannot match its output to the model it has memorised, and its song remains malformed.

D. Neuroscience has since traced the circuitry involved. A pathway running from a region called HVC to another known as RA controls the production of song, while a separate loop passing through Area X is required for learning it but not for performing it once learned. Damage to the learning pathway in an adult whose song has already crystallised leaves that song largely intact — evidence that acquiring a behaviour and executing it depend on partly distinct machinery. A further finding proved unexpectedly influential: in canaries, part of the song system grows and shrinks across the year, which helped overturn the long-held assumption that the adult vertebrate brain generates no new neurons.

E. Because song is copied rather than inherited, it varies from place to place in the manner of a human accent. White-crowned sparrows in neighbouring valleys of coastal California sing recognisably different versions, and a bird raised in one valley will adopt the version it hears rather than the one its parents sang. These dialects are transmitted culturally, drift over time and can be tracked across generations — which makes birdsong one of the few systems in which the evolution of a learned tradition can be observed directly in the wild.

F. Cities have introduced a new pressure. Traffic produces most of its noise at low frequencies, and several species living in urban areas have been found to sing at a higher pitch than their rural neighbours, which reduces the degree to which their song is masked. Whether this represents genuine adaptation or simply an immediate adjustment by individual birds is still argued over, and the change may carry a cost, since a higher-pitched song can be less attractive to females. What is not in doubt is that a learned signal can shift within a few generations — far faster than an inherited one.
